paragraphs: Alyosha went into his elder’s cell with an anxious, aching heart, and he stopped short, almost astonished. He had feared to find a sick man at his last gasp, perhaps unconscious. Instead he saw him sitting up in his chair. He was weak and exhausted, but his face was bright and cheerful. He was surrounded by visitors and taking part in a quiet, joyful conversation. In fact he had got up from his bed only a quarter of an hour before Alyosha arrived. His visitors had gathered in his cell earlier and were waiting for him to wake, having received a most confident assurance from Father Païssy that “the teacher would get up and, as he had himself promised in the morning, talk once more with those dear to his heart.” Father Païssy put implicit trust in this promise, and indeed in every word of the dying elder. If he had seen him unconscious, if he had seen him breathe his last, and still had his promise that he would rise and say good-bye, perhaps he would not have believed even in death. He would still have expected the dead man to recover and keep his promise. In the morning, as he lay down to sleep, Father Zossima had told him firmly: “I shall not die without the delight of another conversation with you, beloved of my heart. I shall look once more on your dear face and pour out my heart to you again.” The monks gathered for this probably last conversation with Father Zossima had all been his devoted friends for many years. There were four of them: Father Iosif, Father Païssy, Father Mihaïl, and a fourth. Father Mihaïl was the warden of the hermitage, a man not very old and far from learned. He was of humble origin, with a strong will and a steadfast faith, austere in appearance but deeply tender, though he plainly hid it, almost as if he were ashamed of it. The fourth, Father Anfim, was a very old, humble little monk of the poorest peasant class. He was almost illiterate and very quiet, and he scarcely spoke to anyone. He was the humblest of the humble, and he looked as though something great and terrible, beyond the reach of his understanding, had frightened him. Father Zossima had a great affection for this timid man and always treated him with marked respect. Yet perhaps there was no one to whom he had said less, although he had spent years wandering about holy Russia with him. That was very long ago, forty years before, when Father Zossima first began his life as a monk in a poor little monastery at Kostroma. Shortly afterward he had gone with Father Anfim on a pilgrimage to collect alms for their poor monastery.

The whole company was in the bedroom, which, as we mentioned before, was very small. There was scarcely room for the four of them to sit round Father Zossima on chairs brought from the sitting room (Porfiry the novice stood). It was already beginning to get dark. The room was lit by lamps and by the candles before the ikons.
Seeing Alyosha standing embarrassed in the doorway, Father Zossima smiled at him joyfully and held out his hand.
“Welcome, my quiet one, welcome, my dear. So here you are too. I knew you would come.”
Alyosha went up to him, bowed down before him to the ground and wept. Something surged up from his heart. His soul was trembling, and he wanted to sob.

“Come, do not weep over me yet,” Father Zossima smiled, laying his right hand on his head. “You see, I am sitting up and talking. Maybe I shall live another twenty years yet, as that dear good woman from Vishegorye, with her little Lizaveta in her arms, wished me yesterday. God bless the mother and the little girl Lizaveta,” he crossed himself. “Porfiry, did you take her offering where I told you?”

He meant the sixty copecks that the good-humored woman had brought him the day before, to be given “to someone poorer than me.” Offerings like this, always of money earned by personal toil, are made as a penance taken on voluntarily. The elder had sent Porfiry the evening before to a widow whose house had burned down lately, and who had gone begging for alms with her children after the fire. Porfiry hastened to answer that he had given the money, as he had been instructed, “from an unknown benefactress.”

“Get up, my dear boy,” the elder went on to Alyosha. “Let me look at you. Have you been home and seen your brother?” It seemed strange to Alyosha that he asked so confidently and precisely about one of his brothers only—but which one? Perhaps, then, he had sent him out both yesterday and today for the sake of that brother.
“I have seen one of my brothers,” answered Alyosha.
“I mean the elder one, the one I bowed down to.”
“I only saw him yesterday. I could not find him today,” said Alyosha.

“Make haste to find him. Go again tomorrow, and make haste. Leave everything and make haste. Perhaps you may still have time to prevent something terrible. Yesterday I bowed down to the great suffering in store for him.”

He was suddenly silent and seemed to be pondering. The words were strange. Father Iosif, who had witnessed the scene yesterday, exchanged glances with Father Païssy. Alyosha could not stop himself from asking:
“Father and teacher,” he began with extreme emotion, “your words are too obscure.... What is this suffering in store for him?”

“Do not ask. Yesterday I seemed to see something terrible ... as though his whole future were expressed in his eyes. A look came into his eyes—so that I was instantly horror-stricken at what that man is preparing for himself. Once or twice in my life I have seen such a look in a man’s face ... reflecting, as it were, his future fate, and that fate, alas, came to pass. I sent you to him, Alexey, because I thought your brotherly face would help him. But everything, and all our fates, are from the Lord. ‘Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone; but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.’ Remember that. You, Alexey, I have many times silently blessed for your face, know that,” added the elder with a gentle smile. “This is what I think of you: you will go forth from these walls, but you will live like a monk in the world. You will have many enemies, but even your foes will love you. Life will bring you many misfortunes, but you will find your happiness in them, and will bless life and make others bless it—which is what matters most. Well, that is your character. Fathers and teachers,” he addressed his friends with a tender smile, “until today I have never told even him why this young man’s face is so dear to me. Now I will tell you. His face has been to me like a remembrance and a prophecy. At the dawn of my life, when I was a child, I had an elder brother who died before my eyes at seventeen. And later, in the course of my life, I gradually became convinced that this brother had been a guidance and a sign from on high for me. For had he not come into my life, I should never, I think at least, have become a monk and entered on this precious path. He appeared to me first in my childhood, and now, at the end of my pilgrimage, he seems to have come to me over again. It is marvelous, fathers and teachers, that Alexey, who resembles him somewhat in face, though not greatly, seems to me so like him in spirit that many times I have taken him for that young man, my brother, mysteriously come back to me at the end of my pilgrimage as a reminder and an inspiration. I positively wondered at so strange a dream in myself. Do you hear this, Porfiry?” he turned to the novice who waited on him. “Many times I have seen in your face a look of mortification that I love Alexey more than you. Now you know why that was so, but I love you too, know that, and many times I grieved at your mortification. I should like to tell you, dear friends, about that youth, my brother, for there has been no presence in my life more precious, more significant and touching. My heart is full of tenderness, and at this moment I look at my whole life as though I were living it through again.”

Here I must observe that this last conversation of Father Zossima with the friends who visited him on the last day of his life has been partly preserved in writing. Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov wrote it down from memory some time after his elder’s death. But whether this was only the conversation that took place then, or whether he added notes of parts of earlier conversations with his teacher, I cannot determine. In his account, Father Zossima’s talk goes on without interruption, as though he told his life to his friends in the form of a story. Yet other accounts leave no doubt that the conversation that evening was general. The guests did not interrupt Father Zossima much, but they too talked, and perhaps even told something themselves. Besides, Father Zossima could not have kept up an uninterrupted narrative. Sometimes he was gasping for breath, his voice failed him, and he even lay down to rest on his bed, though he did not fall asleep and his visitors did not leave their seats. Once or twice Father Païssy interrupted the conversation by reading the Gospel. It is worth noting, too, that none of them supposed he would die that night. That evening, after his deep sleep in the day, he seemed suddenly to have found new strength, which kept him going through this long conversation. It was like a last effort of love, which gave him marvelous energy—but only for a little while, for his life was cut short immediately.... But of that later. I will only add now that I have preferred to confine myself to the account given by Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov. It will be shorter and less tiring, though, as I must repeat, Alyosha took a great deal from earlier conversations and added it to this one.
Notes on the Life of the deceased Priest and Monk, the Elder Zossima, taken down from his own words by Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov.
BIOGRAPHICAL NOTES
_(a)_ _Father Zossima’s Brother_

Beloved fathers and teachers, I was born in a distant province in the north, in the town of V. My father was a gentleman by birth, but of no great consequence or position. He died when I was only two years old, and I do not remember him at all. He left my mother a small wooden house and a fortune, not large, but enough to keep her and her children in comfort. There were two of us, my elder brother Markel and I. He was eight years older than I, of a hasty, irritable temperament, but kind-hearted and never sarcastic. He was remarkably silent, especially at home with me, his mother and the servants. He did well at school but did not get on with his schoolfellows, though he never quarreled, at least so my mother has told me. Six months before his death, when he was seventeen, he made friends with a political exile who had been banished from Moscow to our town for freethinking, and who led a solitary life there. This man was a good scholar who had won distinction in philosophy at the university. Something made him take a liking to Markel, and he used to invite him to visit. The young man spent whole evenings with him that winter, until the exile was summoned back to Petersburg to resume his post, as he had himself asked, for he had powerful friends.

It was the beginning of Lent, and Markel would not fast. He was rude and laughed at it. “That is all silly twaddle, and there is no God,” he said, horrifying my mother, the servants, and me too. For though I was only nine, I too was aghast at hearing such words. We had four servants, all serfs. I remember my mother selling one of the four, the cook Afimya, who was lame and elderly, for sixty paper roubles, and hiring a free servant to take her place.

In the sixth week of Lent my brother, who was never strong and had a tendency to consumption, fell ill. He was tall but thin and delicate-looking, with a very pleasing face. I suppose he caught cold. Anyway, the doctor who came soon whispered to my mother that it was galloping consumption and that he would not live through the spring. My mother began to weep. Careful not to alarm my brother, she begged him to go to church, to confess and take the sacrament, since he was still able to move about. This made him angry, and he said something profane about the church. Yet he grew thoughtful. He guessed at once that he was seriously ill and that this was why his mother was begging him to confess and take the sacrament. Indeed, he had known for a long time that he was far from well. A year before, he had coolly remarked at dinner to our mother and me, “My life will not be long among you, I may not live another year,” which now seemed like a prophecy.

Three days passed, and Holy Week came. On Tuesday morning my brother began going to church. “I am doing this simply for your sake, mother, to please and comfort you,” he said. My mother wept with joy and grief. “His end must be near,” she thought, “if there is such a change in him.” But he was not able to go to church for long. He took to his bed, so he had to confess and take the sacrament at home.

It was a late Easter, and the days were bright, fine and full of fragrance. I remember he used to cough all night and sleep badly, but in the morning he dressed and tried to sit up in an armchair. That is how I remember him sitting, sweet and gentle, smiling, his face bright and joyous in spite of his illness. A marvelous change had come over him; his spirit seemed transformed. The old nurse would come in and say, “Let me light the lamp before the holy image, my dear.” Before, he would not have allowed it, and would have blown it out.
“Light it, light it, dear. I was a wretch to have stopped you doing it. You are praying when you light the lamp, and I am praying when I rejoice at seeing you. So we are praying to the same God.”

Those words seemed strange to us, and mother would go to her room and weep, but when she went in to him she wiped her eyes and looked cheerful. “Mother, do not weep, darling,” he would say, “I have long to live yet, long to rejoice with you, and life is glad and joyful.”
“Ah, dear boy, how can you talk of joy when you lie feverish at night, coughing as though you would tear yourself to pieces?”
“Do not cry, mother,” he would answer, “life is paradise, and we are all in paradise, but we will not see it. If we would, we should have heaven on earth the next day.”

Everyone wondered at his words, he spoke so strangely and positively. We were all touched and wept. Friends came to see us. “Dear ones,” he would say to them, “what have I done that you should love me so? How can you love anyone like me? And how was it that I did not know, that I did not appreciate it before?”

When the servants came in to him he would say again and again, “Dear, kind people, why are you doing so much for me? Do I deserve to be waited on? If it were God’s will for me to live, I would wait on you, for all men should wait on one another.”
Mother shook her head as she listened. “My darling, it is your illness that makes you talk like that.”

“Mother, darling,” he would say, “there must be servants and masters, but if so, I will be the servant of my servants, the same as they are to me. And another thing, mother: every one of us has sinned against all men, and I more than any.”

Mother positively smiled at that, smiled through her tears. “Why, how could you have sinned against all men, more than all? Robbers and murderers have done that, but what sin have you committed yet, that you hold yourself more guilty than all?”

“Mother, little heart of mine,” he said (he had begun using such strange caressing words at that time), “little heart of mine, my joy, believe me, everyone is really responsible to all men, for all men and for everything. I do not know how to explain it to you, but I feel it is so, painfully even. And how is it that we went on living then, getting angry and not knowing?”
So he would get up every day, more and more sweet and joyous and full of love. When the doctor, an old German called Eisenschmidt, came:
“Well, doctor, have I another day in this world?” he would ask, joking.
“You will live many days yet,” the doctor would answer, “and months and years too.”

“Months and years!” he would exclaim. “Why count the days? One day is enough for a man to know all happiness. My dear ones, why do we quarrel, try to outshine each other and hold grudges against each other? Let us go straight into the garden, walk and play there, love, appreciate and kiss each other, and glorify life.”
“Your son cannot last long,” the doctor told my mother as she accompanied him to the door. “The disease is affecting his brain.”

The windows of his room looked out into the garden. Our garden was a shady one, with old trees just coming into bud. The first birds of spring were flitting in the branches, chirruping and singing at the windows. Looking at them and admiring them, he suddenly began begging their forgiveness too: “Birds of heaven, happy birds, forgive me, for I have sinned against you too.” None of us could understand that at the time, but he shed tears of joy. “Yes,” he said, “there was such a glory of God all about me: birds, trees, meadows, sky. Only I lived in shame, and dishonored it all, and did not notice the beauty and glory.”
